claim: Dark exposure (DE) followed by light reintroduction (LRx) reactivates robust synaptic plasticity in adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Dark exposure (DE) followed by light reintroduction (LRx) reactivates robust synaptic plasticity in adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1), which allows subsequent recovery from amblyopia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DE/LRx allows subsequent recovery from amblyopia.
source: Dark exposure (DE) followed by light reintroduction (LRx) reactivates robust synaptic plasticity in adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1), which allows subsequent recovery from amblyopia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior research.

claim: Perisynaptic proteolysis by MMP9 mediates the enhancement of plasticity by LRx in binocular adult mice.
source: Previously we showed that perisynaptic proteolysis by MMP9 mediates the enhancement of plasticity by LRx in binocular adult mice (Murase et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: LRx to adult amblyopic mice induces perisynaptic MMP2/9 activity in deprived and non-deprived V1.
source: Here we show that LRx to adult amblyopic mice induces perisynaptic MMP2/9 activity and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation in deprived and non-deprived V1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LRx to adult amblyopic mice induces extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation in deprived and non-deprived V1.
source: Here we show that LRx to adult amblyopic mice induces perisynaptic MMP2/9 activity and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation in deprived and non-deprived V1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye is sufficient to induce robust MMP2/9 activity at thalamo-cortical synapses in deprived V1.
source: Indeed, LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye is sufficient to induce robust MMP2/9 activity at thalamo-cortical synapses and ECM degradation in deprived V1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye is sufficient to induce ECM degradation in deprived V1.
source: Indeed, LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye is sufficient to induce robust MMP2/9 activity at thalamo-cortical synapses and ECM degradation in deprived V1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The history of visual experience regulates MMP2/9 activity in V1.
source: Two-photon live imaging demonstrates that the history of visual experience regulates MMP2/9 activity in V1, and that DE lowers the threshold for the proteinase activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by two-photon imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: DE lowers the threshold for MMP2/9 activation.
source: Two-photon live imaging demonstrates that the history of visual experience regulates MMP2/9 activity in V1, and that DE lowers the threshold for the proteinase activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by two-photon imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: The homeostatic reduction of the MMP2/9 activation threshold by DE enables visual input from the amblyopic pathway to trigger robust perisynaptic proteolysis.
source: The homeostatic reduction of the MMP2/9 activation threshold by DE enables visual input from the amblyopic pathway to trigger robust perisynaptic proteolysis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Amblyopia affects up to 4% of the world's population.
source: An imbalance in the quality of visual inputs between the two eyes during development induces amblyopia, a developmental disorder affecting up to 4% of the world's population (Levi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Prolonged monocular deprivation induces severe amblyopia in animal models.
source: In animal models, prolonged monocular deprivation induces severe amblyopia, characterized by a significant decrease in the strength and selectivity of neuronal responses in the deprived visual cortex (Fong et al., 2016; Harwerth et al., 1983; Montey et al., 2013) and a significant loss of spatial acuity through the deprived eye (Harwerth et al., 1983; Liao et al., 2011; Montey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Prolonged monocular deprivation causes a significant decrease in the strength and selectivity of neuronal responses in the deprived visual cortex.
source: In animal models, prolonged monocular deprivation induces severe amblyopia, characterized by a significant decrease in the strength and selectivity of neuronal responses in the deprived visual cortex (Fong et al., 2016; Harwerth et al., 1983; Montey et al., 2013) and a significant loss of spatial acuity through the deprived eye (Harwerth et al., 1983; Liao et al., 2011; Montey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Prolonged monocular deprivation causes a significant loss of spatial acuity through the deprived eye.
source: In animal models, prolonged monocular deprivation induces severe amblyopia, characterized by a significant decrease in the strength and selectivity of neuronal responses in the deprived visual cortex (Fong et al., 2016; Harwerth et al., 1983; Montey et al., 2013) and a significant loss of spatial acuity through the deprived eye (Harwerth et al., 1983; Liao et al., 2011; Montey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In rats, spatial acuity in the deprived eye is undetectable following chronic monocular deprivation (cMD) initiated at eye opening.
source: In rats, spatial acuity in the deprived eye is undetectable following chronic monocular deprivation (cMD) initiated at eye opening (Eaton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Following prolonged monocular deprivation, neurons in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) that project to deprived binocular visual cortex have lower metabolism.
source: Additionally, following prolonged monocular deprivation, neurons in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) that project to deprived binocular visual cortex have lower metabolism (Kennedy et al., 1981) and smaller somata (Duffy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Following prolonged monocular deprivation, neurons in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) that project to deprived binocular visual cortex have smaller somata.
source: Additionally, following prolonged monocular deprivation, neurons in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) that project to deprived binocular visual cortex have lower metabolism (Kennedy et al., 1981) and smaller somata (Duffy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: cMD significantly decreases the density of dendritic spines on pyramidal neurons in deprived binocular primary visual cortex (V1b).
source: cMD also significantly decreases the density of dendritic spines on pyramidal neurons in deprived binocular primary visual cortex (V1b) (Montey and Quinlan, 2011) and induces a 60% decrease in the thalamic component of the visually evoked potential (VEP, [Montey and Quinlan, 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: cMD induces a 60% decrease in the thalamic component of the visually evoked potential (VEP).
source: cMD also significantly decreases the density of dendritic spines on pyramidal neurons in deprived binocular primary visual cortex (V1b) (Montey and Quinlan, 2011) and induces a 60% decrease in the thalamic component of the visually evoked potential (VEP, [Montey and Quinlan, 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The loss of synaptic plasticity in the primary visual cortex with age is thought to significantly impede the reversal of amblyopic deficits.
source: The loss of synaptic plasticity in the primary visual cortex with age is thought to significantly impede the reversal of amblyopic deficits (Tailor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Developmental changes in the induction of synaptic plasticity in V1 are regulated by the maturation of fast-spiking basket interneurons (INs) that express the Ca2+ binding protein parvalbumin (PV).
source: Strong evidence demonstrates that developmental changes in the induction of synaptic plasticity in V1 are regulated by the maturation of fast-spiking basket interneurons (INs) that express the Ca2+ binding protein parvalbumin (PV) (Gu et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2013; Morishita et al., 2015; Stephany et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PV+ INs mediate the perisomatic inhibition of pyramidal neurons, thereby exerting powerful control of neuronal excitability and spike-timing dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: PV+ INs mediate the perisomatic inhibition of pyramidal neurons, thereby exerting powerful control of neuronal excitability and spike-timing dependent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about PV+ interneurons.

claim: Developmental changes in synaptic plasticity are associated with the composition and density of the ECM.
source: Developmental changes in synaptic plasticity are also associated with the composition and density of the ECM, comprised of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) and hyaluronic acid, linked via cartilage link protein and tenascins (Carulli et al., 2010; Celio and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 1993; Morawski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ECM is comprised of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) and hyaluronic acid, linked via cartilage link protein and tenascins.
source: Developmental changes in synaptic plasticity are also associated with the composition and density of the ECM, comprised of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) and hyaluronic acid, linked via cartilage link protein and tenascins (Carulli et al., 2010; Celio and Chiquet-Ehrismann, 1993; Morawski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ECM molecules condense into perineuronal nets (PNNs) around a subset of PV+ INs.
source: Importantly, ECM molecules condense into perineuronal nets (PNNs) around a subset of PV+ INs, limiting their structural and functional plasticity by imposing a physical constraint and providing binding sites for molecules that inhibit neurite outgrowth (Dickendesher et al., 2012; Frantz et al., 2016; Stephany et al., 2016; Vo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PNNs limit structural and functional plasticity of PV+ INs by imposing a physical constraint and providing binding sites for molecules that inhibit neurite outgrowth.
source: Importantly, ECM molecules condense into perineuronal nets (PNNs) around a subset of PV+ INs, limiting their structural and functional plasticity by imposing a physical constraint and providing binding sites for molecules that inhibit neurite outgrowth (Dickendesher et al., 2012; Frantz et al., 2016; Stephany et al., 2016; Vo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PNNs accumulate molecules that regulate PV+ IN excitability and maturation.
source: PNNs also accumulate molecules that regulate PV+ IN excitability and maturation (Beurdeley et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Manipulations that reduce the integrity of the ECM/PNNs have been repeatedly shown to enhance plasticity in V1 and elsewhere.
source: Manipulations that reduce the integrity of the ECM/PNNs have been repeatedly shown to enhance plasticity in V1 and elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations and examples provided in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of adult V1 with chondroitinase ABC (ChABC) reactivates robust plasticity in rats.
source: Treatment of adult V1 with the bacterial enzyme chondroitinase ABC (ChABC), which cleaves the CS side chains from the CSPGs, reactivates robust plasticity in rats (Pizzorusso et al., 2006; Pizzorusso et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ChABC cleaves the CS side chains from the CSPGs.
source: Treatment of adult V1 with the bacterial enzyme chondroitinase ABC (ChABC), which cleaves the CS side chains from the CSPGs, reactivates robust plasticity in rats (Pizzorusso et al., 2006; Pizzorusso et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the mechanism of ChABC.

claim: Recovery from MD is incomplete in cats that receive ChABC following eye opening.
source: However, recovery from MD is incomplete in cats that receive ChABC following eye opening (Vorobyov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Enhancement of synaptic plasticity following ChABC treatment has been demonstrated in many brain regions.
source: Enhancement of synaptic plasticity following ChABC treatment has also been demonstrated in many other brain regions (Carstens et al., 2016; Carstens and Dudek, 2019; Gogolla et al., 2009; Kochlamazashvili et al., 2010; Romberg et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of cartilage link protein (Crtl1/Halpn1) prevents the condensation of ECM molecules into PNNs.
source: Genetic ablation of cartilage link protein (Crtl1/Halpn1), which prevents the condensation of ECM molecules into PNNs, prevents the closure of the critical period for ocular dominance plasticity (Carulli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of cartilage link protein (Crtl1/Halpn1) prevents the closure of the critical period for ocular dominance plasticity.
source: Genetic ablation of cartilage link protein (Crtl1/Halpn1), which prevents the condensation of ECM molecules into PNNs, prevents the closure of the critical period for ocular dominance plasticity (Carulli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dark rearing from birth produces a parallel delay in the maturation of ECM/PNNs and the closure of the critical period.
source: Dark rearing from birth produces a parallel delay in the maturation of ECM/PNNs and the closure of the critical period (Lander et al., 1997; Mower, 1991; Pizzorusso et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Robust juvenile-like synaptic plasticity can be restored in adults by complete visual deprivation through DE followed by LRx.
source: However, robust juvenile-like synaptic plasticity can be restored in adults by complete visual deprivation through DE followed by LRx (He et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DE/LRx induces an increase in perisynaptic activity of MMP9 and subsequent proteolysis of extracellular targets in binocular adult mice.
source: Our previous work demonstrated DE/LRx induces an increase in perisynaptic activity of MMP9 and subsequent proteolysis of extracellular targets in binocular adult mice (Murase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The proteinase activity induced by LRx is perisynaptic and enriched at thalamo-cortical synapses.
source: The proteinase activity induced by LRx is perisynaptic and enriched at thalamo-cortical synapses.
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: The reactivation of structural and functional plasticity by DE/LRx is inhibited by pharmacological blockade and genetic ablation of MMP9.
source: Importantly, the reactivation of structural and functional plasticity by DE/LRx is inhibited by pharmacological blockade and genetic ablation of MMP9.
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: Mmp9-/- mice are resistant to enhancement of plasticity by DE/LRx.
source: Although Mmp9-/- mice are resistant to enhancement of plasticity by DE/LRx, treatment with hyaluronidase activates structural and functional plasticity in adults.
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: Treatment with hyaluronidase activates structural and functional plasticity in adult Mmp9-/- mice.
source: Although Mmp9-/- mice are resistant to enhancement of plasticity by DE/LRx, treatment with hyaluronidase activates structural and functional plasticity in adults.
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors.

claim: In adult rats rendered severely amblyopic by cMD from eye opening to adulthood, DE followed by reverse occlusion enables recovery of the VEP amplitude and dendritic spine density in deprived V1b.
source: In adult rats rendered severely amblyopic by cMD from eye opening to adulthood, DE followed by reverse occlusion enables recovery of the VEP amplitude and dendritic spine density in deprived V1b (He et al., 2007; Montey and Quinlan, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Subsequent visual training promotes a full recovery of visual acuity in the deprived eye in adult rats rendered severely amblyopic by cMD.
source: Subsequent visual training promotes a full recovery of visual acuity in the deprived eye (Eaton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A similar reactivation of plasticity by DE has been reported in several species.
source: A similar reactivation of plasticity by DE has been reported in several species (Duffy and Mitchell, 2013; Stodieck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DE lowers the threshold for activation of MMP2/9 by light, such that LRx to the deprived eye is sufficient to induce perisynaptic proteolysis at thalamo-cortical synapses and ECM degradation in deprived visual cortex.
source: Here we use a biomarker that reports the activity of MMP2/9 in vivo to examine the effects of DE/LRx on extracellular proteolysis in amblyopic mice. We show that DE lowers the threshold for activation of MMP2/9 by light, such that LRx to the deprived eye is sufficient to induce perisynaptic proteolysis at thalamo-cortical synapses and ECM degradation in deprived visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in MMP2/9 biomarker puncta density in deprived and non-deprived V1b.
source: However, LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in MMP2/9 biomarker puncta density (deprived: 67.0 ± 8.0 puncta/0.01 mm2, non-deprived: 70.2 ± 14.7 puncta/0.01 mm2) and puncta intensity (deprived: 55.6 ± 2.6 pixel, non-deprived: 54.6 ± 2.8 pixel) in deprived and non-deprived V1b, with no difference in puncta size (deprived: 0.88 ± 0.06 μm2, non-deprived: 0.86 ± 0.06 μm2, n = 6 subjects, One-way ANOVAs, density F(3, 19)=6.7, p=0.003; intensity F(3, 19)=8.4, p=0.0009; size F(3, 19)=0.52, p=0.67; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1A.

claim: LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in MMP2/9 biomarker puncta intensity in deprived and non-deprived V1b.
source: However, LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in MMP2/9 biomarker puncta density (deprived: 67.0 ± 8.0 puncta/0.01 mm2, non-deprived: 70.2 ± 14.7 puncta/0.01 mm2) and puncta intensity (deprived: 55.6 ± 2.6 pixel, non-deprived: 54.6 ± 2.8 pixel) in deprived and non-deprived V1b, with no difference in puncta size (deprived: 0.88 ± 0.06 μm2, non-deprived: 0.86 ± 0.06 μm2, n = 6 subjects, One-way ANOVAs, density F(3, 19)=6.7, p=0.003; intensity F(3, 19)=8.4, p=0.0009; size F(3, 19)=0.52, p=0.67; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1A.

claim: LRx did not change MMP2/9 biomarker puncta size in deprived and non-deprived V1b.
source: However, LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in MMP2/9 biomarker puncta density (deprived: 67.0 ± 8.0 puncta/0.01 mm2, non-deprived: 70.2 ± 14.7 puncta/0.01 mm2) and puncta intensity (deprived: 55.6 ± 2.6 pixel, non-deprived: 54.6 ± 2.8 pixel) in deprived and non-deprived V1b, with no difference in puncta size (deprived: 0.88 ± 0.06 μm2, non-deprived: 0.86 ± 0.06 μm2, n = 6 subjects, One-way ANOVAs, density F(3, 19)=6.7, p=0.003; intensity F(3, 19)=8.4, p=0.0009; size F(3, 19)=0.52, p=0.67; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1A.

claim: LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in biomarker co-localization with VGluT2 in deprived and non-deprived V1b, indicating an increase in MMP2/9 activity at thalamo-cortical synapses.
source: LRx induced a significant and parallel increase in biomarker co-localization with VGluT2 in deprived and non-deprived V1b, indicating an increase in MMP2/9 activity at thalamo-cortical synapses (deprived: 161 ± 6%, non-deprived: 199 ± 17%, n = 6, 5, 6, 6 subjects for cMD dep, cMD non, LRx dep, LRx non, respectively; One-way ANOVA, F(3, 19)=9.5, p=0.0005; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1B.

claim: The LRx-induced increase in co-localization of biomarker and VGluT2 was observed at PV+ neuronal somata and in PV- locations, suggesting widespread activation of perisynaptic MMP2/9.
source: The LRx-induced increase in co-localization of biomarker and VGluT2 was observed at PV+ neuronal somata and in PV- locations, suggesting widespread activation of perisynaptic MMP2/9 (dep: 625.3 ± 50.1%, non: 484.1 ± 35.2% for PV+, dep: 361.7 ± 34.5%, non: 537.1 ± 85.4% for PV-, n = 4 subjects; One-way ANOVA, PV+ F(3, 12)=17.33, p=0.00012; PV- F(3, 12)=56.17, p<0.0001; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1C.

claim: DE followed by 2 hr of LRx significantly increased the concentration of active MMP9 in parallel in deprived and non-deprived V1b of adult cMD mice.
source: Quantitative immunoblot analysis showed that DE followed by 2 hr of LRx significantly increased the concentration of active MMP9 in parallel in deprived and non-deprived V1b of adult cMD mice (% of cMD dep: 133.04 ± 9.1%; non: 131.37 ± 8.9%; n = 7, eight subjects for cMD and LRx, respectively; One-way ANOVA, F(3, 26)=5.6, p=0.004; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunoblot data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 1D.

claim: MMP9 has several extracellular targets, including aggrecan (Agg) the predominant CSPG in the ECM of the adult mammalian cortex.
source: MMP9 has several extracellular targets, including aggrecan (Agg) the predominant CSPG in the ECM of the adult mammalian cortex (Mercuri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: LRx induced a significant decrease in the intensity of WFA and Agg, but not PV labeling, 250 μm-400 μm from the cortical surface.
source: LRx induced a significant decrease in the intensity of WFA and Agg, but not PV labeling, 250 μm-400 μm from the cortical surface (mean ± SEM; % of cMD, WFA dep 54.3 ± 3.5, non 46.3 ± 3.4, One way ANOVAs, F(3, 26)=32, p<0.0001; Agg dep 62.3 ± 3.1, non 54.3 ± 4.5, F(3, 26)=10, p=0.0001; PV dep 105.0 ± 6.9, non 96.4 ± 4.5; F(3, 26)=0.4, p=0.75; n = 7, 7, 8, 8 subjects for cMD dep, cMD non, LRx dep, LRx non, respectively; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in WFA and Agg staining was observed at PV+ and PV- locations suggesting widespread degradation of ECM upon LRx.
source: Line scans of triple-labeled images revealed that the decrease in WFA and Agg staining was observed at PV+ and PV- locations suggesting widespread degradation of ECM upon LRx (% of cMD, WFA PV+ dep 56.3 ± 2.1, non 55.4 ± 2.1; One-way ANOVAs, F(3, 309)=40.3, p<0.0001; WFA PV- dep 69.5 ± 1.9, non 66.8 ± 1.3; F(3, 309)=30.1, p<0.0001; Agg PV+ dep 61.9 ± 1.4, non 60.2 ± 1.4; F(3, 309)=29.4, p<0.0001; Agg PV- dep 77.1 ± 1.2, non 71.0 ± 1.3; F(3, 309)=18.7, p<0.0001; n (subjects, ROIs)=(5, 77 , 5, 73 , 5, 81 , 5, 82), for cMD dep, cMD non, LRx dep, LRx non, respectively; *p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 2D.

claim: LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye induced an increase in MMP2/9 biomarker density and intensity in layer four in deprived V1b relative to non-deprived V1b.
source: LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye induced an increase in MMP2/9 biomarker density and intensity in layer four in deprived V1b (contralateral to the cMD eye, ipsilateral to eye patch) relative to non-deprived V1b (ipsilateral to the cMD eye, contralateral to eye patch; density: 208.8 ± 23.1% of non, n = 6 subjects, p=0.014; intensity: 161.1 ± 22.9% of non, n = 6 subjects, p=0.046, Student's T-test), with no change in biomarker puncta size (111.7 ± 14.8% of non, n = 6 subjects, p=0.56, Student's T-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 3A.

claim: LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye induced a significant increase in the co-localization of MMP2/9 biomarker puncta with VGluT2 in deprived relative to non-deprived V1b.
source: Similarly, LRx restricted to the amblyopic eye induced a significant increase in the co-localization of MMP2/9 biomarker puncta with VGluT2 in deprived relative to non-deprived V1b (dep: 57.8 ± 3.5%; non: 33.4 ± 5.0%, n = 6 subjects, p=0.0026, Student's T-test; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 3B.

claim: LRx to the deprived eye alone induced a decrease in the mean fluorescence intensity of WFA and Agg in layer 4 of deprived V1b relative to non-deprived V1b.
source: LRx to the deprived eye alone induced a decrease in the mean fluorescence intensity of WFA and Agg in layer 4 of deprived V1b (contralateral to cMD eye, ipsilateral to eye patch) relative to non-deprived V1b (ipsilateral to cMD eye, contralateral to eye patch; quantified 250 μm - 400 μm from the cortical surface: WFA: 48.7 ± 7.0% of non, n = 5 subjects, p=0.0009; Agg: 50.2 ± 16.1% of non, n = 5 subjects, p=0.02, Student's T-test), with PV fluorescence unchanged (83.3 ± 17.7% of non-deprived, n = 5 subjects, p=0.4, Student's T-test; Figure 4A–C, WFA and IHC of PV in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 4.

claim: MMP2/9 biomarker expression is low in the adult visual cortex, indicating that ambient light does not typically stimulate activation of this proteinase.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that MMP2/9 biomarker expression is low in the adult visual cortex, indicating that ambient light does not typically stimulate activatioin of this proteinase (Murase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The robust induction of MMP2/9 activity by reintroduction to ambient light suggests that DE may lower the threshold for MMP2/9 activation.
source: The robust induction of MMP2/9 activity by reintroduction to ambient light, therefore, suggests that DE may lower the threshold for MMP2/9 activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that LRx induces MMP2/9 activity after DE.

claim: Stimulation with moderate intensity light (300 cd/m2) induced an increase in raw fluorescence and biomarker ΔF/F of the biomarker, but not co-localized GFP, in DE subjects.
source: In contrast, stimulation with moderate intensity light (300 cd/m2; equivalent to luminance in the laboratory) induced an increase in raw fluorescence and biomarker ΔF/F of the biomarker, but not co-localized GFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a significant increase in biomarker fluorescence in DE subjects following moderate intensity light stimulation.
source: Population data reveals a significant increase in biomarker fluorescence in DE subjects following moderate intensity light stimulation (repeated measure ANOVA, F(1, 22), p<0.001; n = 12 puncta from three subjects; *p<0.001, Tukey-Kramer post hoc test; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 5D.

claim: The change in biomarker fluorescence was similar to that observed following higher intensity light stimulation (150,000 cd/m2).
source: The change in biomarker fluorescence was similar to that observed following higher intensity light stimulation (150,000 cd/m2, equivalent to direct sunlight at noon; One-way ANOVA, F(2, 40)=6.3, p=0.0042, n = 12, 12, 19 puncta from three subjects each, for 0, 300, 150,000 cd/m2, respectively; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results and Figure 5E.

claim: Moderate intensity light stimulation (300 cd/m2) was insufficient to induce an increase in biomarker fluorescence in control (0 hr DE) or dark-adapted (18 hr DE) subjects.
source: Importantly, moderate intensity light stimulation (300 cd/m2) was insufficient to induce an increase in biomarker fluorescence in control (0 hr DE) or dark-adapted (18 hr DE) subjects (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-delivery of MMP9 inhibitor with biomarker 24 hr prior to LRx inhibited the increase in biomarker fluorescence by high intensity light.
source: Co-delivery of MMP9 inhibitor (MMP9i, 5 nM 4 μl at 100 nl/min) with biomarker 24 hr prior to LRx inhibited the increase in biomarker fluorescence by high intensity light (n = 13 puncta from 3 subjects for 0 and 150,000 cd/m2; Student's T-test; p=0.13).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis presented in the results.

claim: DE lowers the threshold for light-induced MMP2/9 activation in the adult visual cortex.
source: Together this demonstrates that DE lowers the threshold for light-induced MMP2/9 activation in the adult visual cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-photon imaging data presented in the results.

claim: Activity-dependent induction of perisynaptic proteolysis is a powerful mechanism to couple experience with the activation of synapse-specific plasticity.
source: Activity-dependent induction of perisynaptic proteolysis is a powerful mechanism to couple experience with the activation of synapse-specific plasticity.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the adult visual cortex, the threshold for activation of MMP2/9 is high and basal activity is low, favoring stability over plasticity.
source: Indeed, in the adult visual cortex, the threshold for activation of MMP2/9 is high and basal activity is low, favoring stability over plasticity.
